## GitHub workflow
- **Default: local-first** (as of 2026-06-16; it's faster than the API). Claude edits files in a local clone that lives **inside the connected project folder**, runs the test suites in the sandbox, then hands Lane a `git add -A && git commit -m "…" && git push` to run on his Mac.
- **The sandbox runs read-only `git`, never mutating `git`.** Inspection commands such as `git diff`,
  `git show`, `git log`, and `git ls-files` work and are preferred for evidence. Commands that create locks,
  update refs or the index, commit, clone, or push remain Mac-side because FUSE lock/hardlink operations fail
  and the sandbox cannot authenticate a push.
- **GitHub API / MCP (`push_files`, `create_or_update_file`) is the backup** — use it when Lane is away from his Mac or no local clone is available. (The PAT-carrying MCP tools still work; they're just no longer the default.)
- **Commit email must be the GitHub `noreply` alias.** Lane's account has "Block command line pushes that expose my email" enabled, so any commit stamped with `lanebecker@gmail.com` is rejected on push with `GH007: Your push would publish a private email address`. Each clone's `user.email` must be his noreply address (`<id>+lanebecker@users.noreply.github.com`, from github.com/settings/emails). Set it globally — `git config --global user.email "<id>+lanebecker@users.noreply.github.com"` — so every clone inherits it. If a commit was already made with the wrong email: `git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit` then push.
- **Every fix commit carries `Closes #NNN`.** The bullet below says to FILE findings as issues before acting on them — and said nothing about closing them. The asymmetry bites: 2026-07-20, ELEVEN R7 fixes shipped to `main` with their issues still open, because the commit messages were long and descriptive and omitted the one mechanical keyword. Put `Closes #NNN` in the handoff command block itself, at the point the message is written; a rule Claude merely intends to apply at commit time is one it has already demonstrated it will drop. Keep a finding-ID → issue-number map (e.g. `r7-issue-map.tsv`) so reconciliation is one grep, not 108 title comparisons.
- **Milestones + issues via `gh` (Mac-side scripts).** The GitHub MCP creates/closes/labels/assigns issues but has **no milestone-creation tool**, so Claude hands Lane `gh` commands to run on his Mac. Create a milestone (there's no native `gh milestone` subcommand) via the API: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/milestones -f title="…" -f description="…" -f state=open` (prints the new milestone's `number`). Assign issues by **title**: `gh issue edit <n1> <n2> … --repo <owner>/<repo> --milestone "<title>"` (takes multiple issue numbers in one call). ⚠️ Interactive **zsh doesn't treat `#` as a comment** by default → strip `#` comment lines from pasted blocks or each errors `command not found: #` (harmless — the real commands still run).

## Memory conventions
- **Keep a `log.md`** — an append-only change history, newest at the bottom, each line prefixed with an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp. `scripts/sync-shared-facts.py` creates one per project and records each sync; add your own notable changes too. In a Cowork space, keep it at `memory/log.md`.
- **Timestamp every memory entry.** Any knowledge/memory file with YAML frontmatter carries an ISO-8601 `timestamp` field; the sync script warns about `memory/*.md` entries that don't.

## Engineering workflow (code/tech projects only — skip for non-tech)
- **Review + test after every completed step, unprompted.** On finishing any step that changes code: (a) review the change for correctness/regressions, (b) add or update tests covering it, (c) run the suite — *before* moving on. Don't wait to be asked; this is how the app stays maintainable.
- **Confirm a design change with Lane before building the next thing on it — unless he's said "just go" for that stretch** *(Lane, 2026-07-28)*. How something LOOKS or BEHAVES for the user — a card's fields, a control's placement, copy, an interaction — is Lane's to approve, not mine to assume. When a step adds or alters one, show it and get the nod BEFORE starting the work that depends on it. ⚠️ Earned: mid-feature I silently dropped a pre-filled field Lane had approved on the mockup, and later ran a manual review in place of the mandated independent narrow-audit agent — both caught by Lane, after the dependent work was already moving. Confirming first turns a rebuild into a one-line fix; it is the SPEC-verdict instinct aimed at the DESIGN, not the diff.
- **End-of-phase adversarial cold audit (agent-based).** After wrapping a significant chunk (e.g., the end of a phase), spawn an **independent subagent** to cold-audit the codebase with no inherited context — hunting for efficiency wins, architecture improvements, significant refactors, and bugs. Agent-based on purpose so Claude can **argue with it**: pressure-test and debate the findings rather than accepting them wholesale, then act on the ones that survive scrutiny.
- **Record code-audit findings as GitHub issues/milestones BEFORE acting on them.** After the cold audit + argue-down triage, file the surviving findings as issues in the relevant repo (group into a milestone if it's a coherent batch) before starting fixes — so nothing's lost mid-remediation. Code audits only; documentation-audit findings are fixed in-flow (no issues needed).
- **Then a documentation cold audit.** After the code audit, cold-audit ALL docs (CLAUDE.md, design docs, READMEs, CHANGELOGs, memory, log.md) to confirm every change is fully mapped and nothing slipped through the cracks.
- **Then a VERIFICATION PASS on the artifact itself** *(Lane, 2026-07-20, R7)*. The audits above examine the code; **nobody examines the document the work is then driven from** — and a defect there multiplies by every issue filed from it. So every audit report, implementation plan or spec gets **one more independent no-context agent whose target is the DOCUMENT**, before it is handed over or acted on. Dispatch rules, each earned: give it **the user's original request verbatim** (otherwise SPEC has nothing to check scope against); tell it to find where the document is **WRONG, not whether it agrees** — wrong things first and at length, "do not soften, this is about to become N issues"; require it to **recompute every stated count** rather than read them, **diff the finding-ID set against the wave/plan set** (IDs in neither or in both), **spot-check every CRITICAL plus a random sample** against the cited file AND line, hunt **overstatements AND understatements** (asking for one direction biases the answer — R7's best catches were understatements), and specifically hunt **"claimed missing but actually present"**. Record what it catches **in** the document, struck through — a silently deleted false finding gets re-found next round with no memory of why it died. ⚠️ Earned: on R7 it returned **SPEC: FAIL** on a doc about to become 108 issues — a headline count typed wrong in all four fields *in a document asserting "computed, never typed" three paragraphs above*; one outright false finding; and an unmeasured premise the doc had exempted from its own measure-first rule, which when finally measured **killed the finding it was gating** (R7-30 dropped HIGH→LOW; the prescribed fix would have been pure churn on the setting that decides whether push works). **The first correction of the count was also wrong.** Full catch list: `log.md`, 2026-07-20. Scope to substantial deliverables — on a three-paragraph summary this is ceremony.
- **Reviews carry TWO verdicts: spec compliance, then code quality** *(adopted from obra/superpowers, 2026-07-17)*. Every review or audit of a change reports (a) **SPEC** — the change does exactly what the plan/finding/issue text said, nothing missing, nothing extra — and (b) **QUALITY** — it is well-built. A review missing either verdict is incomplete. Apply the SPEC verdict to **remediations** especially: check the fix against the original finding's text before judging the code (every audit round's largest source of findings has been the previous round's remediation). Two sub-rules: never tell an auditor what NOT to flag or pre-rate a finding's severity in the dispatch — the argue-down happens AFTER the report, never inside the prompt; and verify an implementer subagent's "done" against the actual diff, never its self-report.
- **Adversarially audit your OWN remediation diff, BEFORE it is committed** *(Lane, 2026-07-25, R8 Wave 8)*. The three audit rules above target the CODEBASE (end-of-phase), the DOCUMENT (the verification pass), and the PREVIOUS round's remediation (the SPEC verdict). None of them catches the fix you wrote ten minutes ago — which is the most dangerous artifact in the room, because it is fresh, it is confident, and its tests were written by the same mind that wrote the bug. So every non-trivial remediation gets one more independent no-context agent whose ONLY instruction is *break this*. ⚠️ Earned: five R8 fixes shipped with **759/759 node + 44/44 Playwright green** — the counts *on that day*, not a live total; a dated anecdote in a rule that says "compute, don't type" is still a number to run rather than read (the app node suite is 768 as of 2026-07-25) — seven of them written RED-first and mutation-killed — and the cold agent still found a **CRITICAL cross-account data write**, a version-stagnation that let a stale peer clobber records, and a fix that turned a shipped "(sandbox)" button into the live flow that mints a real forwarding address. **One of my own mutation-kill tests was faithfully pinning the security regression.** A green suite proves the code does what you meant; it cannot tell you that what you meant was wrong. Four dispatch rules, each load-bearing:
  - **REQUIRE AN EXECUTED REPRODUCTION.** "Write a script that actually demonstrates any bug you claim; a bug you cannot reproduce is a hypothesis and you must label it as such." That one sentence is the difference between six actionable findings and thirty plausible ones — each arrives with its own before/after table, so triage takes minutes.
  - **Enumerate the ATTACK SURFACES** in the prompt (this function now runs at a new point in another's lifecycle; this gate changed its default; this new state survives a session reset). A generic "review this diff" earns a generic answer.
  - **Ask it to label PRE-EXISTING vs INTRODUCED.** Half the value is knowing what is yours. A pre-existing defect it surfaces is a NEW ISSUE to file, not something to smuggle into the current wave.
  - **Budget it deliberately — never skip it for cost.** A full pass is ~20 min on a 2-core sandbox, largely because the executed-reproduction rule makes it serial. That is the price; pay it. Then ARGUE IT DOWN as with any cold audit: of six findings, four accepted, one rejected as pre-existing/out-of-scope, one accepted only as a comment correction — because a comment that overclaims a benefit the callers do not deliver is itself a defect.
- **THEN A SECOND, NARROW PASS OVER THE FIXES THE FIRST PASS CAUSED** *(Lane, 2026-07-25, R8 Wave 8)*. Its own step, because it has its own TRIGGER: not "the diff is finished" but **"I just changed code because a reviewer told me to."** Those edits are the most dangerous in the whole change — written fast, written under the flattering impression of having just been corrected, and never themselves reviewed by anyone. The remediation-of-a-remediation is where this codebase's worst defects have always lived; that is the same law as the SPEC-verdict bullet above, applied one loop tighter and within a single sitting.
  - **Scope it to ONLY the reworked hunks, and cap it hard**: "~20 tool calls, at most 2 reproductions, everything else may be reported as HYPOTHESIS — that is expected and fine." ~7 minutes against ~20 for a full pass, so cost is never the reason to skip it. Tell it explicitly that this is attempt #2 and that a rework is the highest-risk part of the diff, not the safest — otherwise it spreads itself evenly and re-audits what the first pass already cleared.
  - ⚠️ **Earned twice, in opposite directions.** On Wave 8 the second pass found five more things on fixes that were already green and mutation-verified — including a version adoption guarded on `doc.version` but NOT on `docVersion`, re-opening the very cross-session class (R7-13/#506) the fix cited three lines above, and a comment claiming a user-facing benefit that every caller discards. On Wave 9 the pass was **SKIPPED** — by the same session that had written this rule into this file hours earlier — because it was buried inside a bullet about cost. Nothing in the fixes was re-checked before the CHANGELOG. Hence the promotion to a step with its own name and its own trigger.
  - The stopping rule is convergence, not a count: run a third pass only if the second returned something that required a non-trivial code change. Two clean-ish rounds is done.
- **Write plans to the junior-engineer bar** *(adopted from obra/superpowers, 2026-07-17)*. Implementation plans are written for "an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, and no project context" — who is also exactly the no-context cold auditor that will later read them. Exact file paths; complete code in every step that changes code; exact commands with expected output. Banned placeholders: "TBD", "add appropriate error handling", "write tests for the above" (without the tests), "similar to Task N" (repeat the content — tasks get read out of order). Self-review the finished plan: (1) spec coverage — every requirement points at a task; (2) placeholder scan; (3) name/type consistency across tasks.
- **Three failed fixes = stop and question the architecture** *(adopted from obra/superpowers, 2026-07-17)*. Count fix attempts on any bug. At the third failure the problem is structural, not hypothetical — do not attempt fix #4; stop and question the pattern (with Lane, if it implies real refactoring). Sibling rule for multi-component pipelines (Gmail→Worker→inbound→parse→commit): instrument the component boundaries — log what enters and exits each layer — to locate the failing component BEFORE forming any hypothesis.
- **Silent data loss: REPRODUCE the loss before fixing it** *(2026-07-20, R7-05/R7-13)*. The mutation loop proves a test CAN fail; it cannot prove a fix is CORRECT under concurrency, and it is blind to "this change corrupts data." So for any bug that deletes or corrupts rows, first write the test that makes rows disappear on TODAY's code and SEE IT RED — then fix. A fix shipped against a bug that was never reproduced is a hypothesis with a green tick.
- **Two explanations = stop and MEASURE** *(2026-07-20, #454)*. The sibling of the rule above: that one counts fixes, this counts EXPLANATIONS. When one surprising observation gets a second competing explanation, stop mid-sentence and name the measurement that would discriminate them; if none exists, say so rather than picking the nicer story. Earned the hard way: four explanations for one 200 (Pages precedence → nothing deployed → edge cache → apex pinned to an old deployment), three of them wrong, ~2h, plus a whole-repo restructure justified by the first one and written into three files as established fact. One `curl -I` was available from the first 200. ⚠️ **The four rules below were extracted OUT of this bullet on 2026-07-21, because being buried in it was itself the failure mode.** Three memories already said "measure, don't reason" — read-the-live-object, verify-the-finding-before-fixing-it, instrument-the-boundaries — and all three were loaded and NONE fired, because each triggers on a different ACT: editing, receiving a finding, attempting a fix, explaining an observation. A trigger that cannot be found does not fire. That is why these are separate counters rather than one principle.
- **Premise before mechanism.** When a fix "doesn't work", first PROVE the fix is present in the thing under test — pushed? deployed? the right URL/row/binary? — before explaining why it failed.
- **Know what the instrument REPORTS vs what it INTERPRETS.** Prefer raw signal (`curl -sI` for status + `cf-cache-status` + `age`; the live pg catalog; executing the function) over anything that renders or summarises. And ask whether the probe could even return *different* output for the two hypotheses — if not, it is not evidence.
- **A tool's success message reports ITS criterion, not yours.** Name your goal as an observable NUMBER before running anything, then check that number rather than the green tick; where possible, make the tool print the number instead of relying on remembering this. Earned three times: `memory-index.py --fix` printed "clean" while making the file it was run to shrink 105 bytes BIGGER; the served-surface test passed by asserting the RULES EXISTED while the site was wide open; and `sync-shared-facts.py` reported "Updated: 0 — everything already up to date" immediately after its source changed (it had in fact synced on a prior invocation, but "0" was taken as "nothing happened" until the target file was actually grepped).
- **A verification fetch can CACHE the broken state and then confirm it.** Cache-bust every check.
- **A cloud sandbox may have very few CPU cores, which caps multi-agent parallelism** *(2026-07-23, R8 audit)*. The Workflow tool runs at most `min(16, cores - 2)` subagents at once, so a wide fan-out serializes instead of running in parallel — on a **2-core** box a 34-agent audit crawled toward ~2 hours before it was re-scoped to ~13. Before sizing ANY Workflow/subagent fan-out, run `nproc`, and budget wall-clock by TOTAL agent-count (× per-agent minutes ÷ concurrency), not by how wide it looks: consolidate slices and batch the verifiers rather than spawning one agent per item. (Sibling sandbox fact, same round: the in-sandbox GitHub token is fine-grained/API-only — it reads via the GitHub MCP but cannot `git clone` a private repo, so stage code by tarring it through the device bridge.)

Design prototype and production renderer for a vinyl now-playing display (1024×600 Waveshare, Raspberry Pi).

## Repository Structure

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `design/` | React/Babel design prototype — browser-runnable, design tool only |
| `src/` | Production Python/Pillow/pygame renderer |
| `src/display/assets/fonts/` | Bundled OFL fonts (Inter Tight, Newsreader, JetBrains Mono) used by the production renderer |
| `PRODUCT.md` | Product spec |
| `DESIGN.md` | Design system and production handoff spec |
| `design/.impeccable/design.json` | Design system tokens for impeccable tooling |

## Prototype vs. Production

The `design/` directory is a **design tool, not production code.** It runs in a browser via React/Babel CDN imports and is used for design iteration and review. All geometry and specs in `DESIGN.md` are derived from the prototype.

The `src/` directory contains the **production renderer** — Python/Pillow/pygame targeting the Raspberry Pi. When a design decision from the prototype is ready to ship, it gets translated here.

## Running the Prototype

Open `design/index.html` in a browser (serve from the `design/` directory — local `file://` works for most features). No build step.

## Key Design Constraints

- Display: 1024×600px target device. The renderer is actually **resolution-independent** — it reads width/height from config and scales every constant proportionally (`s = min(width/1024, height/600)`); there are no hard-coded breakpoints, but there is also no fixed artboard. (A-10)
- Font hierarchy: Inter Tight 600 72px (song) / Inter Tight 500 48px (artist) / Newsreader italic 32px (album) / JetBrains Mono 13px (catalog) / 12px (chip) / 11px (label) — all at the 1024×600 reference, scaled by `s`
- DisplayPalette: 5 values — bg, surface, accent, text, muted — 1s lerp on track change
- Full-Opacity Rule: `p.muted` never gets additional `opacity` stacked on top; it is contrast-clamped to ≥4.5:1 at palette-extraction time (and re-clamped during the lerp). `accent` is clamped the same way, because the renderer draws the album title in `accent` (so it is a text role) — via `ensure_contrast_hue_preserving` (lifts lightness, keeps the cover's hue) rather than the blend-to-white used for the neutral `muted`. Both are clamped against `text_background(bg, surface)` — the gradient's brightest pixel (`GRADIENT_TEXT_PEAK`), **not flat `bg`** — since that is the brightest surface text can land on (DISP-1 / DISP-2, Wave 4).
- Hue Diversity Rule (**NOT a production feature — deliberately deferred 2026-06-19, #73**): the prototype's `data.js` is hand-tuned for ≥60° OKLCH hue separation between album accents, but the production renderer does **not** implement it and is not planned to. `accent` is simply the most-saturated quantized color of the current cover, in isolation (lightness-lifted for WCAG contrast per the Full-Opacity Rule above, but **hue-preserved** — so it stays the cover's own color, never a synthetic one) — kept authentic to the artwork on purpose. Enforcing cross-album separation would make the accent synthetic (a color not in the cover) and the palette order-dependent (breaking the pure `url → palette` cache); revisit only if same-hue runs prove distracting on the physical display. (was A-1)
- WCAG AA: 4.5:1 minimum contrast on all text
